title: Give Every Worker One Task at the Smallest Total Price

concept.title: Assign the workers in order: the set of used tasks tells how many workers are done
body: There are `n` workers and `n` tasks. Every worker gets **exactly one task** and every task goes to **exactly one worker**; giving the task `j` to the worker `i` costs `cost[i][j]`. Find the assignment with the smallest total cost. For the costs `9 2 7 / 6 4 3 / 5 8 1` the best total is 9 (worker 1 gets task 2, worker 2 gets task 1, worker 3 gets task 3: 2 + 6 + 1). With 16 workers there are 16! = 20 trillion assignments.

Assign the workers **in order**: worker 0 first, then worker 1, and so on. After the first `k` workers have their tasks, what matters for the rest is only **which tasks are taken**, a set of `k` tasks, written as a bitmask. Let `best(mask)` be the smallest cost of giving the tasks in `mask` to the first `popcount(mask)` workers. The worker number `k = popcount(mask)` takes the task `j` that is **not** in `mask`: **`best(mask | (1 << j)) = min(best(mask) + cost[k][j])`**. The answer is `best(all tasks)`. The worker is not part of the state, because the number of tasks taken tells which worker is next.

body.code:
INF = 10 ** 18
best = [INF] * (1 << n)
best[0] = 0
for mask in range(1 << n):
    if best[mask] == INF: continue
    k = bin(mask).count("1")                  # the next worker
    if k == n: continue
    for j in range(n):
        if not mask >> j & 1:
            nm = mask | (1 << j)
            best[nm] = min(best[nm], best[mask] + cost[k][j])
print(best[(1 << n) - 1])

body: There are `2^n` states with `n` choices each: 1 million steps for 16 workers. Making a quantity (here the number of the worker) a function of the state, instead of an extra dimension, saves a factor of `n` in time and memory. (The *Hungarian algorithm* solves the same problem in O(n^3), which wins for bigger `n`, but the bitmask DP is easier to write and to adapt to extra rules.)

statement: There are `n` workers and `n` tasks; giving the task `j` to the worker `i` costs `cost[i][j]`. Each worker gets exactly one task and each task goes to exactly one worker. Print the smallest possible total cost.
inputFormat: The first line has `n`: the number of workers and the number of tasks.
Each of the next `n` lines has `n` numbers: `cost[i][j]` is the price of giving the task `j` to the worker `i`.

examples.note: Worker 1 takes task 2 (cost 2), worker 2 takes task 1 (6), worker 3 takes task 3 (1): 9.

hints: Assign the workers in order; the set of taken tasks is a bitmask.
The next worker is the one with the number popcount(mask).

explanation: best(mask) is the smallest cost of giving the tasks of the bitmask mask to the first popcount(mask) workers; the next worker takes one of the tasks that are not in the mask, so every state extends to the states with one more task. The answer is best of the full mask.

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n = int(input())
cost = [list(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(n)]

INF = 10 ** 18
full = (1 << n) - 1
best = [INF] * (1 << n)
best[0] = 0
for mask in range(full):
    cur = best[mask]
    if cur == INF:
        continue
    k = bin(mask).count("1")
    row = cost[k]
    for j in range(n):
        if not (mask >> j) & 1:
            nm = mask | (1 << j)
            v = cur + row[j]
            if v < best[nm]:
                best[nm] = v
print(best[full])
